final_proof:
Let \(\mathcal D(\mathbb R)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\), and let \(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)\) be arbitrary. Each \(\delta_n\) is integrable (and hence defines a regular distribution). Indeed, since \(n>0\), the substitution \(t=nx\) gives
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,dx
=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dt}{1+t^2}
=1.
\]
In particular, the normalization expected of a delta sequence holds (and \(\delta_n\ge 0\)). More importantly, applying the same substitution to the action on \(\varphi\) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle\delta_n,\varphi\rangle
&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac n\pi\frac{\varphi(x)}{1+n^2x^2}\,dx\\
&=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(t/n)}{1+t^2}\,dt.
\end{aligned}
\]
For every fixed \(t\in\mathbb R\), continuity of \(\varphi\) at \(0\) gives \(\varphi(t/n)\to\varphi(0)\). If \(M=\|\varphi\|_\infty\), then for every \(n\) and \(t\),
\[
\left|\frac1\pi\frac{\varphi(t/n)}{1+t^2}\right|\leq \frac{M}{\pi(1+t^2)}.
\]
The function on the right is integrable on \(\mathbb R\), because \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(1+t^2)^{-1}dt=\pi\). Therefore the dominated convergence theorem gives
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\langle\delta_n,\varphi\rangle
=\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\varphi(0)}{1+t^2}\,dt
=\varphi(0).
\]
By definition, the Dirac delta distribution satisfies \(\langle\delta,\varphi\rangle=\varphi(0)\). Since the displayed convergence holds for every \(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R)\), it follows that \(\delta_n\to\delta\) in \(\mathcal D'(\mathbb R)\). Thus \((\delta_n)_{n\geq1}\) is a delta sequence in the asserted distributional sense.
